works.abstract: Priming effects (PE) on soil organic matter (SOM) mineralization depend strongly on the type of carbon substrates added. It is crucial to understand the PE induced by various carbon substrates for predicting SOM dynamics and soil-atmosphere carbon feedback. We conducted a meta-analysis of 8015 observations from 283 articles to evaluate how carbon substrates (plant residues, root exudates, biochar, and degradable microplastics) regulate the mineralization of SOM through PE. Results demonstrated that all these types of carbon substrates increased SOM mineralization, which induced a positive PE. Plant residues induced the highest average PE, followed by root exudates, biochar, and degradable microplastics. Compared to soils without carbon substrate inputs, the rate of SOM mineralization increased by 113% in soil with cellulose-rich non-woody residues, whereas it increased by only 25% in soil with lignin-rich woody residues. The mineralization of SOM increased by organic acids (151%) was greatest in root exudates, followed by monosaccharides (60%) and polysaccharides (12%). The strong mineralization induced by organic acids was probably related to the release of more mineral nutrients by reducing soil pH. The PE on SOM mineralization by woody biochar with high aromatic carbon content (48%) was greater than that of non-woody biochar with high alkyl carbon content (43%). Microplastics with rapidly degradable polyhydroxyalkanoates induced more SOM mineralization (258%) than polybutylene succinate (61%) and polybutylene adipate-co-terephthalate (21%). The SOM priming was positively correlated with soil clay and incubation moisture, and negatively correlated with soil organic carbon, total nitrogen, soil C:N ratio, dissolved organic carbon, microbial biomass carbon, carbon input rate, incubation temperature, and soil depth. These results show that the positive PE is ubiquitous in soil ecosystems; its magnitude is linked intrinsically to the physicochemical characteristics and source of exogenous carbon substrate.
works.title: Priming Effects on Soil Organic Matter Mineralization by Carbon Substrates: A Global Meta‐Analysis

works.abstract: Abstract Soil microplastics (MPs) pollution is a global ecological environment threat. Although biodegradable plastics are designed substitutes for nonbiodegradable plastics, biodegradable MPs in soil is a carbon source that can increase or decrease soil organic matter (SOM) mineralization through priming effect. Soil nitrogen (N) availability can alter the priming effects by orchestrating the microbial growth and metabolism, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive, especially under global warming. Based on incubation experiments using long‐term N‐fertilized soils, we found that the polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) MPs‐induced priming effect was co‐regulated by the fungal N mining from SOM and bacterial necromass mineral protection of SOM, and warming amplified this phenomenon. The PHA‐induced priming effect ranged from 7% to 45%, highest in soil without N fertilizer input, followed by low‐N and high‐N fertilizer input soils. Warming increased the priming effect by 13%−15% in soil without N, whereas decreased the priming intensity by 2%−3% in high‐N soil. Specifically, warming increased microbial biomass production, and thus carbon use efficiency (CUE) by increasing dissolved organic carbon resulting from PHA decomposition. In soil without N, high CUE promoted fungal dominance, stimulating N mining and SOM loss. In high‐N soil, high CUE promoted bacterial driven necromass accumulation, enhancing SOM stabilization through microbial and mineral carbon pumps. Therefore, N availability in PHA‐contaminated soil modulates microbial community dynamics (bacterial and fungal) under warming, ultimately determining loss and sequestration of SOM. These findings highlight that long‐term N fertilization application can mitigate SOM loss caused by biodegradable MPs pollution, and provide critical insights for industrial and agricultural management.
works.journal: Soil Science Society of America Journal
works.title: Soil nitrogen availability regulates the warming effect on the priming effect induced by polyhydroxyalkanoate microplastics
